steps.explanationAfterStep: The OMe lone pair makes the CH₂ beside it the diene's most nucleophilic end (it has the largest coefficient in the diene's HOMO), and the ester makes the acrylate's CH₂ the most electrophilic end (largest coefficient in its LUMO). Joining those two ends puts OMe and the ester 1,4 round the new ring: the “para” product. A 2-substituted diene gives “para”; a 1-substituted diene gives “ortho”.

Correct arrows, but this is the minor “meta” isomer: the diene's nucleophilic CH₂ has bonded to the acrylate carbon next to the ester, the less electrophilic end. Most of the product forms the other way round.

title: Regiochemistry of a Diels–Alder reaction
subtitle: 2-Methoxybutadiene and methyl acrylate: the “para” product
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 34

reactants.caption: 2-methoxybuta-1,3-diene + methyl acrylate
hintTiers: The methoxy oxygen pushes its lone pair into the diene; the ester pulls electrons out of the acrylate. Which end of the diene is the more nucleophilic, and which carbon of the acrylate is the more electrophilic?

Imagine the methoxy lone pair pushing towards the CH₂ next to the carbon carrying OMe: that CH₂ is the nucleophilic end. It bonds to the CH₂ end of methyl acrylate, the carbon that conjugate additions attack. Three arrows, one step.

Arrow 1: from the C=C π bond carrying OMe to a new bond between its CH₂ end and the CH₂ of methyl acrylate. Arrow 2: from the other diene π bond to the bond between the two middle diene carbons. Arrow 3: from the acrylate C=C π bond to a new bond between its CH carbon (next to the ester) and the far CH₂ of the diene.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Both partners are unsymmetrical, so they can join two ways round. Draw the cycloaddition that gives the main product.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The carbon carrying OMe is a middle carbon of the diene: it does not make a new σ bond. Only the two CH₂ ends of the diene do.
Only the two CH₂ ends of the diene make new bonds; the middle carbons end up joined by the new C=C.
The ester C=O takes no part. In a Diels–Alder reaction the dienophile's C=C is what the diene bonds to; the ester only makes it more reactive and decides which way round it adds.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the nucleophilic CH₂ of the diene bonds to the CH₂ end of the acrylate. Now finish the ring of moving electrons: two more arrows in the same step.

mechanismSummary: The cycloaddition is concerted, but its transition state is unsymmetrical: the bond between the best-matched ends forms ahead of the other. The methoxy group raises the diene's HOMO and puts its largest coefficient on the neighbouring CH₂; the ester lowers the acrylate's LUMO and puts its largest coefficient on the far CH₂. Matching large with large gives the “para” (1,4) product. The enol ether in the product can later be hydrolysed to a ketone.
